unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Trametinib for Dogs with Histiocytic Sarcoma
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description: The purpose of this research is to investigate a new anti-cancer drug, trametinib, that specifically ‘targets’ growth signals found in cancer cells from companion (pet) dogs. This study will determine the anti-tumor efficacy of trametinib in dogs with histiocytic sarcoma. We will measure and document how much the cancer shrinks upon treatment, and how the drug helps improve the patients’ outcome and life expectancy. Additionally, the study will test whether markers in the genes within the tumor can predict the response from treatment, which in the future can help select those dogs that are more likely to respond positively to treatment. Finally, in a simple blood test we will determine whether effective drug levels are present in the patient.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Incidence of hypercoagulability and thromboembolism in dogs with surgically treated primary hepatocellular and adrenal neoplasia
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
The goal of this study is to characterize the hemostatic abnormalities in dogs with primary hepatocellular or primary adrenal cancer undergoing surgical removal and to determine when their hypercoagulability (increased tendency for blood to clot) resolves post-operatively. Additionally, we aim to determine the incidence of thromboembolism (blood clots) in hypercoagulable patients diagnosed with primary hepatocellular or primary adrenal cancer following tumor removal.


Dogs with suspected primary hepatocellular or adrenal neoplasia will undergo standard-of-care procedures, including blood work (CBC, chemistry, and PT/PTT) and CT of the abdomen. Upon enrollment, a TEG and fibrinogen level will be obtained before surgery for the study. Dogs will return in 10-14 days for re-check full-body CT and blood work (PCV/TS, TEG, PLT, fibrinogen). Dogs will return in 15-21 days for re-check blood work. Dogs will continue to return for recheck blood work (PCV/TS, TEG, fibrinogen, and PLT) until their hypercoagulability, based on an elevated TEG G-value, resolves.


If a dog remains hypercoagulable at the 10-14 day post-surgery visit, they will be asked to come back for 3 and/or 4-week post-surgery visits until their hypercoagulability resolves. If a dog remains hypercoagulable at the 4-week post-surgery visit, it will present as needed for 6, 8,12, and/or 16-week post-operative visits until their hypercoagulability resolves. If a dog remains hypercoagulable at the 16-week post-operative visit, blood work re-checks will move to a monthly schedule until resolution is achieved. No future visits are required once a dog becomes normocoagulable. No future visits are required, and monthly blood work will discontinue if a dog remains hypercoagulable at 6 months post-operative (day 182).


The study will cover the cost of your dog's pre-operative chest and post-operative abdominal and chest computed tomography (CT) scan. Additionally, the study will cover the cost of each recheck examination fee and the cost of performing blood work (TEG, PCV/TS, platelet count, and fibrinogen) pre-and post-operatively.


Routine blood work (PT/PTT, CBC, chemistry panel, blood type prior to surgery) will not be covered by the study. The study does not cover the cost of your dog's other preoperative workup (primary tumor biopsy/FNA, pre-operative abdominal CT, thoracic radiographs, etc.), primary tumor removal, hospitalization, post-operative care, or additional oncologic care (radiation therapy or chemotherapy). Costs associated with adverse events (including but not limited to hematoma, and incisional complications) are not covered by the study.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Clinical Testing of Canine T cells Engineered to Target Osteosarcoma and Soft Tissue Sarcoma in Combination with Oral Immunotherapy
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
The purpose of this clinical trial is to evaluate the safety and anti-cancer activity of fibroblast activation protein (FAP) targeted chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells, alone or in combination with orally administered immunotherapy drugs, in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma. FAP is a protein that is expressed on the surface of tumor cell and can be recognized by a T cell. CAR T cells are when a patient’s own cancer fighting white blood cells are modified to express a receptor which binds a specific molecule expressed on the surface of a tumor cell. The two oral immunotherapy drugs being used in combination with FAP CAR T cells (losartan and toceranib [Palladia]) have already been extensively evaluated in a prior trial in dogs with bone cancer and have demonstrated considerable anti-cancer activity, with minimal toxicity. Studies in rodent models of cancer and in vitro in human and canine OS cell lines have indicated that FAP CAR T cells can exert robust killing of canine OS cells and may complement the activities of toceranib and losartan. Therefore, this trial is designed to determine whether FAP CAR T cells are safe alone and in combination with losartan and toceranib, and if losartan and toceranib can improve tumor infiltration of FAP CAR T cells.


At the start of the study, dogs will have blood drawn (~3 ½ tablespoons) to be used for generation of the CAR T cells. Dogs will also be sedated to have a small sample of their tumor taken for study purposes. They will return 10 days later for an exam, bloodwork, and for oral chemotherapy to reduce the number of normal lymphocytes (a type of white blood cell) to maximize the effectiveness of the CAR T cells. A second dose of chemotherapy will be given at home by the owner the following day. Dogs will then return 14 days after the initial visit for an exam, blood and urine tests, blood collection for study purposes, and CAR T cell infusion. The infusion is given over 15 minutes, and then dogs will stay in the hospital until the end of the day for monitoring. Dogs will return 3 and 7 days later for an exam, blood and urine tests, and blood collection for study purposes. Fourteen days after the CAR T infusion, the tumor will be removed surgically. Visits will be required 2 and 6 weeks after surgery for an exam, blood/urine tests, and blood collection for the study. The study is complete after the visit 6 weeks post-surgery (total study duration of 10 weeks).


Some dogs enrolled in the study will receive two oral immune modulating drugs (toceranib and losartan) for the first ~4 weeks of the study. These will be given at home by the owners 1-2 times daily. Owners will know ahead of time whether or not dogs will be receiving these drugs.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Canine Liver Tumor Study
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
North Carolina State University College of Veterinary Medicine is currently enrolling canine patients that have 1-2 liver tumors into a clinical trial that is using a new therapy called INSPIRE, which uses electrical pulses to safely destroy the cells within a tumor.


This study has two treatment group:


One group of study applicants should have 1-2 liver tumors measuring between 1-3cm. Potential candidates will come in through the Medical Oncology service at NC State Veterinary hospital for a screening appointment to check eligibility for enrollment. If the patient is eligible for the study and their tumors are eligible for surgical resection, the patients in this group will return one week later for a one time INSPIRE treatment followed by liver lobectomy a week later to remove the tumors.


The second group of study applicants should have 1-2 liver tumors measuring between 1-3cm. Potential candidates will come in through the Medical Oncology service at NC State Veterinary Hospital for a screening appointment to check eligibility for enrollment. If the patient is eligible for the study and the tumors are not eligible for surgical resection, patients will return one week later for a one time INSPIRE treatment. Patients will then be monitored over a 9-month period which includes five recheck appointments, during which patients will receive a CT scan and bloodwork to monitor the tumors.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Treating Metastatic Cancer with PD-1 inhibitor and Targeted Immunotherapy
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Metastatic disease prevents a unique clinical setting especially when the patients is still stable. Options are limited for treatment but may include oral and IV chemotherapy options. With the advent of PD-1 inhibitors, we are now looking to combine the inhibitor with either Telomerase or HER2 immunotherapy in combination as the combined therapies should improve response while minimizing adverse effects and battling the cancer through specific mechanisms.


Trends Cancer 2023 Jul;9(7):543-553.

 doi: 10.1016/j.trecan.2023.04.002. Epub 2023 Apr 27.

Immune mechanisms of toxicity from checkpoint inhibitors

S Jennifer Wang 1, Stephanie K Dougan 2, Michael Dougan 3


Abstract

Immunotherapy has changed the treatment landscape for cancer over the past decade. Inhibitors of the immune checkpoint proteins cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen (CTLA)-4, programmed death (PD)-1, and PD ligand 1 (PD-L1) can induce durable remissions in a subset of patients with metastatic disease. However, these treatments can be limited by inflammatory toxicities that can affect any organ system in the body and in some cases can be life threatening. Considerable progress has been made in understanding the drivers of these toxicities as well as effective management strategies. Further research into understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms that drive toxicity will enable better prediction of toxicity and development of optimized therapies for these toxicities that avoid interfering with antitumor immunity. In this review, we discuss our current understanding of the inflammatory toxicities from immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) and propose optimal treatment strategies for these toxicities.


Clinical protocol: Patients will be treated with standard of care anti-PD1 SOP: Administered as an intravenous (IV) infusion over at least 30 minutes either manually or with a constant rate syringe pump. Repeat administration every 2 weeks for up to 10 treatments. Antihistamine administered intramuscularly (IM) 15-30 minutes before treatment to prevent or reduce the severity of infusion-related reactions, 20-30 minutes following administration, patients will be sedated with propofol, dexdomitor and O2 via intubation for GET (see below).


GET: DNA Plasmid: The N-10-4B electrode to be inserted into the cranialis tibialis after immediate injection of dTERT or dHER2 DNA/plasmid. Minimal bleeding to be controlled with direct pressure.


Antisedan to be administered IM.


*Regarding the use of this technology (gene-electrotransfer or GET) as the method for vaccine delivery, numerous studies, including the one below, support the improved immune response compared to injections under the skin or in muscle.


Pharmaceutics. 2023 Jul; 15(7): 1981.

Published online 2023 Jul 19. doi: 10.3390/pharmaceutics15071981

PMCID: PMC10385748

PMID: 37514166

What We Learned about the Feasibility of Gene Electrotransfer for Vaccination on a Model of COVID-19 Vaccine

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: COSMyc- IT Trial- Canine Oncology Study for Myc Inhibition Tolerability Trial
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Myc (a family of transcription factors encompassing c-, N-, and L-Myc) is a pleiotropic, evolutionarily conserved transcription factor. Myc is one of the most frequently amplified oncogenes in most (perhaps all) human cancers (Dang 2012, Whitfield 2017) and often correlates with aggressiveness of the disease (Wolfer 2010; Lee 2015). In breast cancer, Myc is overexpressed in 30–50% of high-grade tumors, is markedly elevated in triple-negative breast cancer and even further elevated in tumors that display a drug-resistant phenotype (Fallah 2017). In non-small cell lung cancer, Myc amplification is found in up to 30% of malignancies (Ahmadzada 2018; Kalkat 2017).


A new novel peptide that inactivates Myc has been developed and is currently in human trials. The goal of this study is to determine the tolerability and feasibility of administering this novel peptide to dogs with cancer to inform future efficacy studies.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Combination chemotherapy (Doxorubicin-Temozolomide with or without propranolol) in dogs with Hemangiosarcoma
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description: The objective of this study is to investigate the effectiveness of combining doxorubicin and temozolomide with or without propranolol in dogs with hemangiosarcoma. The use of either doxorubicin alone as a treatment for hemangiosarcoma has been studied, and studies with propranolol (historically used to treat heart disease) have shown promise as an added treatment against hemangiosarcoma, however, survival times still remain quite low. A sister drug to Temozolomide, DTIC, has shown promise in improving survival times, however side effects and the long administration times have created challenges with the use of DTIC in dogs. Temozolomide is administered orally and is historically well tolerated in dogs. We are hopeful that survival times can be further improved using a combination approach to treatment, with combination of both intravenous and oral treatments and improved tolerability. Dogs with hemangiosarcoma of the spleen, liver, heart or intramuscular region will be considered for inclusion in this study.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Pilot Study for a New Quasiorganelle Therapy in Dogs with Histiocytic Sarcoma
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Histiocytic sarcoma is an aggressive cancer in dogs that often does not respond well to standard treatments like chemotherapy or radiation. While some dogs experience benefits, these treatments affect many cells at once and cannot adapt as a tumor changes. New research shows that cancer closely interacts with the immune system and surrounding tissues, suggesting that better treatments may need to work inside cells, not just target them from the outside. Quasiorganelle therapy is an experimental approach that aims to do this by using weakened, non-disease-causing bacteria derived from Listeria monocytogenes to deliver helpful genetic instructions directly into immune and tumor cells, with the goal of improving how the body recognizes and responds to cancer.


The first group (8 dogs) will receive quasiorganelle therapy alone. Their tumor will be measured and they will receive the quasiorganelle infusion. They will then be observed for up 4 days at the MSU Veterinary Medical Center and blood and fecal samples will be taken at set timepoints. The dogs will return for treatment once weekly for 4 doses followed by 2 weeks off. This schedule will then be repeated two more times for a total of 16 weeks of treatment. Imaging to determine alterations in tumor size will be repeated at the end of each 4 week treatment period.

The second group (8 dogs) will receive quaisorganelle therapy that includes gene therapy. Their treatment and monitoring schedule will be identical to that of the first group.

Following the 16 week treatment period, dogs will return for evaluation every 4 weeks or until progressive disease is documented.


Please note: While enrolled, dogs should not live with anyone who is pregnant or planning to become pregnant.

Please note: All treatments and relevant follow up must be performed at Michigan State University College of Veterinary Medicine. Investigational treatment will not be sent to outside clinics.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Treatment of Canine Sarcoma with FAP CAR T-cells (FAP CAR-T Study)
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
CAR T cell therapy has fundamentally changed how certain cancers are treated. By reprogramming a patient's own T lymphocytes to express a receptor targeting a protein on tumor cells, it directs the immune system to destroy them, producing durable remissions in blood cancers once refractory to conventional treatment.


These benefits have yet to reach veterinary patients, and some cancers remain especially hard to treat with immunotherapy. Sarcomas can be very resistant to standard treatment across many species, including dogs. Led by investigators at Colorado State University, we are testing CAR T cells engineered against FAP, a protein highly expressed in many sarcomas, in pet dogs. We are evaluating both the therapy's activity and its side effects. Advancing this work meets a real clinical need for companion animals while accelerating progress for human patients as well.


In this study, we will test a new treatment for dogs with sarcomas. As the tumor has to be biopsied, this study is best for sarcomas that are external or on the outside of the body.


IACUC: 24677

Study number: VCCT-26-017

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Combination of electrochemotherapy and gene therapy with canine IL-12
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is an advanced treatment in veterinary oncology. It has been routinely used in dogs for treating mast cell tumors, carcinomas and soft tissue sarcomas, in cats for SCC, carcinomas and sarcomas and in horses for sarcoid tumors. ECT is a local ablative technique which has a good local anti-tumor control in dogs (up to 70%) and in cats (up to 80%) and in horses up to 100% but limited impact on distant tumors and metastasis. Therefore, there is a need for a combination therapy which could provide local control with a systemic effect to battle cancer spread. Interleukin 12 is a potent immune stimulator that works by increasing IFN gamma which has an anti-tumor effects through the activation of cytotoxic cells such as natural killer cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes. IL-12 also up-regulates antigen presenting cells making the tumor cells recognizable to the immune system. Several clinical studies have already been performed treating different canine tumors by electro-genetransfer with a plasmid encoding IL-12. Results showed increased systemic IL-12 and IFN gamma with an effect on distant metastasis .

Procedure: The treatment consists of electrochemotherapy with bleomycin (intravenously) and gene-electrotransfer (GET) of IL-12 (intra-lesional). The treatment will be performed in patients under a short general anesthesia. Depending on the tumor volume and the response the treatments will be repeated every 3-4 weeks. Responses will be followed with physical exam and imaging (X-rays or CT). Electrochemotherapy will be performed using direct intra-tumoral application of IL-12 (2mg per patient) and the intravenous application of bleomycin (standard dose). The study is based on multiple publications showing benefit with this combination with control of the cancer including metastasis and minimal to no adverse effects to the patients.


References: 1. Pavlin, D. et al. Electrogene therapy with interleukin-12 in canine mast cell tumors. Radiol Oncol 45, 3139 (2011). 2.Tozon, N., Pavlin, D., Sersa, G., Dolinsek, T. & Cemazar, M. Electrochemotherapy with intravenous bleomycin injection: an observational study in superficial squamous cell carcinoma in cats. J. Feline Med. Surg. 16, 291299 (2014). 3.Tamzali, Y. et al. Methods Mol Biol 423, 319325 (2008). 6.Cemazar, M. et al. Efficacy and safety of electrochemotherapy combined with peritumoral IL-12 gene electrotransfer of canine mast cell tumours. Vet. Comp. unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Dual Energy CT to Assess Bone Mineral Density in Dogs with Osteosarcoma Undergoing Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs and, while amputation followed by systemic chemotherapy is the standard of care, it may not be the most appropriate treatment option for all dogs or it may not meet the goals of individual owners. Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) has been utilized to kill tumor cells while leaving the affected limb intact showing good primary tumor control rates. The biggest risk with using SBRT in this setting is the potential for pathologic fracture of the affected limb. Here we plan to use a dual energy CT for radiation planning and to quantify bone mineral density (BMD) both before and after SBRT to assess changes that happen with SBRT treatment. BMD measures calcium and other minerals. In theory, the more mineral, the denser and stronger the bone is and less likely it is to break. In addition, we will measure bone breakdown markers before and after treatment to determine how these are correlated with the BMD and response to treatment.


Once enrolled, dogs will have blood and urine collected for bone breakdown markers followed by 3 doses (or fractions) of SBRT. On the third and final fraction, dogs will receive the first dose of standard of care chemotherapy (carboplatin). Two weeks after chemotherapy, your dog will need to have a complete blood count performed to assess response to chemotherapy as well as blood and urine collected for the bone breakdown markers. At each dose of chemotherapy, a total of 6, blood and urine will be collected to assess trends in these markers. At the time of the final chemotherapy treatment, an additional dual energy CT will be performed to assess the changes that happen to the bone after treatment. Once chemotherapy is complete, it is recommended that your dog return every 8 weeks for chest x-rays; blood and urine will be collected for the study at the 1st 3 visits post-chemotherapy. At any change in lameness or concern for progression of disease, it is expected that your dog will return to CSU for assessment and evaluation of the bone markers.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Mammary tumors in cats
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Surgery is the most common treatment used for mammary cancer in cats. The pathologist determines whether surgery has removed all cancer cells many days after the procedure. We need rapid and accurate testing during surgery to detect residual cancer to decrease cancer recurrence and the necessity for repeated surgery or treatments.


Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) is an imaging technology that uses near-infrared light waves to generate real-time, high-resolution images of the microscopic structure of tissues, specifically looking at the organization of the tissues. We have performed some initial evaluations using this optical coherence tomography for detection of residual cancer, which has had very encouraging results.


Cats will undergo surgery to remove their tumor; following removal, the tumor will be scanned with polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography to assess the surgical margins for residual cancer cells. The specimen will then undergo thorough histopathological assessment.


The overall purpose of the study is to evaluate a new imaging method to detect cancer cells left behind following removal of mammary tumors in client-owned cats undergoing surgery. This technology has been used successfully in human breast cancer surgery, providing microscopic assessment of surgical margins within minutes. Identifying a rapid and thorough imaging method to detect any remaining cancer cells during surgery for mammary tumors will support targeted treatment management decisions and improve outcomes for cats and dogs with cancer.


Pet owners are financially responsible for all costs associated with evaluation and surgery. Each pet owner receiving surgery at OSU will receive a $70 credit to their account to cover the costs of the histopathology evaluation.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Electrochemotherapy for Bone Cancer
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Electrochemotherapy is a valuable anti-cancer therapy in both human and veterinary patients. Until recently, there was no electrode to allow treatment of bone lesions. Veterinary Oncology Services (www.petcancerinformation.com) has a bone electrode used in human applications (see below).


Curr Oncol. 2022 Mar 4;29(3):1672-1682. doi: 10.3390/curroncol29030139.

Electrochemotherapy Is Effective in the Treatment of Bone Metastases

Laura Campanacci 1, Luca Cevolani 1, Francesca De Terlizzi 2, Laura Saenz 3, Nikolin Alì 1, Giuseppe Bianchi 1, Davide Maria Donati 1


Abstract

Bone metastases induce pain, risk of fracture, and neural compression, and reduced mobility and quality of life. Electrochemotherapy (ECT) is a minimally invasive local treatment based on a high-voltage electric pulse combined with an anticancer drug. Preclinical and clinical studies have supported the use of ECT in patients with metastatic bone disease, demonstrating that it does not damage the mineral structure of the bone and its regenerative capacity, and that is feasible and efficient for the treatment of bone metastases. Since 2009, 88 patients with bone metastasis have received ECT at the Rizzoli Institute. 2014 saw the start of a registry of patients with bone metastases treated with ECT, whose data are recorded in a shared database. We share the Rizzoli Institute experience of 38 patients treated with ECT for a bone metastasis, excluding patients not included in the registry (before 2014) and those treated with bone fixation. Mean follow-up was 2 months (1-52). Response to treatment using RECIST criteria was 29% objective responses, 59% stable disease, and 16% progressive disease. Using PERCIST, the response was 36% OR, 14% SD, and 50% PD with no significant differences between the two criteria. A significant decrease in pain and better quality of life was observed at follow up.


Clinical protocol: Patient will be anesthetized and the lytic area of bone to be treated identified. Using a Jamshidi bone needle, a core will be created allowing placement of the linear bone electrode into the lesion. Once in place, targeted electrochemotherapy will be applied into the lytic lesion. Bleomycin will be injected IV and after 8 minutes the pulse will be sent into the bone lesion allowing a transient opening of the cell membrane. 2- 3 treatments will be completed and the area wrapped upon recovery.


Follow up imaging in 4 and 8 weeks with radiographs.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Single Radiation Treatment for Dogs with Transmissible Venereal Tumor
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Canine transmissible venereal tumor (TVT) is an infectious cancer that can be spread between dogs, often through grooming behaviors or sexual contact. This cancer can be found worldwide, but is most common in Central and South America, Africa, and Asia. In the United States, this cancer is most commonly seen in animals rescued from other parts of the world, or in free-roaming pets in very remote areas.


Treatment for this cancer involves once-weekly injections of chemotherapy, which are given until the cancer is resolved. For patients who cannot undergo this chemotherapy treatment, finding alternate therapies can be invaluable. We know that this cancer responds well to older forms of radiation therapy; however, we aim to determine if a single treatment with modernized radiation can provide similar treatment outcomes with fewer visits compared to chemotherapy.


Dogs enrolled in this study will receive a single dose of radiation therapy, followed by recheck visits 7 days and 28 days after treatment. At each of these visits, patients will have tumor measurements and small samples of their masses collected with a needle for analysis. Patients complete the study on day 28 or if their tumor progresses after radiation treatment. At that time, patients with persistent tumors are eligible to receive $1000 towards the cost of standard chemotherapy treatment.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Novel Immunotherapy for Cats with Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Oral squamous cell carcinoma is a very difficult cancer to treat in cats and is often fairly advanced before it is detected. This clinical trial will be examining the effectiveness of a new type of immunotherapy for treating this disease in cats, which is based on very promising data from two squamous cell carcinoma trials conducted recently in horses at CSU. This new treatment is designed to stimulate the body’s own immune defenses to attack the tumor cells and cause tumor regression or elimination. In this particular trial, even stopping the tumor from growing (rather than full elimination) would be considered a success. This immunotherapy drug has been tested previously in cats, and is generally well-tolerated, with few side-effects, but it has only been evaluated in one cat with oral squamous cell carcinoma previously. The treatment has however been extensively evaluated in horses with squamous cell carcinoma, with a high degree of success. In this study, we will evaluate this novel immunotherapy in cats with oral SCC to determine how well the treatment works and how well it is tolerated by cats.


Cats will receive four injections of the LTN immunotherapy into their tumor, which are given once every three weeks. Cats must be put under anesthesia for these injections. While under anesthesia, cats will have CT scans and tumor biopsies performed prior to starting treatment, at the time of the third injection, and 3 weeks after the 4th injection (CT only). Blood tests (complete blood count and chemistry profile) will also be performed at these visits. Study participation is completed after the visit that is 3 weeks after the last injection. A total of 5 visits and anesthetic episodes are required for this study.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: PRISM Trial: Precision Research Integrating Symptoms and Molecular Biology in Canine Glioma
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
High-grade gliomas are aggressive brain tumors that are difficult to treat in dogs. While surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy may help some dogs, we still have much to learn about why some tumors respond better to treatment than others.


The purpose of this study is to better understand brain tumors in dogs by collecting information about each dog's health, MRI findings, tumor characteristics, and in some dogs, how they respond to radiation treatment. By studying many dogs with naturally occurring brain tumors, we hope to identify patterns that will help veterinarians diagnose these tumors more accurately, predict how they may behave, and develop more effective treatments in the future.


Although participation in this study may not directly benefit every dog, the information gained will help improve the care of dogs diagnosed with brain tumors and advance the development of new treatment options. Every dog that participates helps us learn more about brain tumors and brings us one step closer to improving treatment and quality of life for future dogs facing this disease.


IACUC: 24619

Study number: VCCT-26-014


The study will provide $3000 toward initial diagnotic tests or radiation therapy for your pet.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Ethos Precision Medicine Umbrella Study for Hemangiosarcoma (Ethos-PUSH)
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description: Canine splenic hemangiosarcoma is an aggressive cancer with limited treatment options available. Dogs presenting with this disease often have spontaneous internal bleeding that results in sudden onset of weakness or collapse. Although this is a common consequence for hemangiosarcoma, any other tumor of the spleen can spontaneously bleed resulting in these same changes. Dogs who have a bleeding splenic tumor must undergo surgery to remove the spleen (called splenectomy). This procedure both removes the source of life-threatening hemorrhage and provides tissue samples for making a final diagnosis. Roughly 40% of dogs have benign splenic disease causing the internal bleeding and will be cured with surgery alone. Many of the remaining dogs will have hemangiosarcoma as the cause of their bleeding and will require chemotherapy following surgery to delay or prevent metastatic disease. For dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma, the combination of surgery and chemotherapy has been estimated to provide median survival times of 4-9 months with only a small percentage of dogs surviving to 2 years. Ethos-PUSH embarks on a journey to improve the outcome of canine hemangiosarcoma by furthering our understanding of this disease. Dogs confirmed to have hemangiosarcoma will be randomized to receive 1 of 4 treatments. These treatment groups include standard therapies and novel therapies that have been selected as potential targets against previously defined genomic alterations in hemangiosarcoma. Treatment arms will be compared to determine a best protocol, which will serve as the benchmark for future treatment studies. Furthermore, tumor and blood samples will be collected and serve as platforms for nationwide collaborations to improve the molecular understanding of this disease and match molecular biomarkers with treatment response to specific therapeutics. This comprehensive approach is designed to bring about curative outcomes for dogs suffering from this aggressive cancer. unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Minimally Invasive Metastasectomy in Canines (MIMIC) Trial
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description: Following surgical removal of the primary tumor and treatment with chemotherapy, the spread of cancer to the lungs (metastasis) is the most common cause of mortality in dogs with many tumors. A distinctive feature of lung metastases in human patients is the surprising benefit that can result from surgical removal of the lung metastases. The use of surgery to manage lung metastases in dogs has been described but is not commonly used due to the presumed post-surgical complications associated with conventional open chest surgery (thoracotomy). Innovations in minimally invasive surgery have created a new opportunity to include surgical removal of lung metastases with a reduced potential of complications when compared to the conventional thoracotomy techniques. Conventional thoracotomy techniques can be replaced by thoracoscopy, a surgical technique using miniature incisions in the chest to allow for removal of lung metastases with the assistance of a magnified video camera. This approach has the potential to significantly minimize the pain, potential complications, and recovery time in patients compared to what is observed with conventional thoracotomy techniques. Using minimally invasive surgery, specifically video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS), we predict patients will be recovered from the procedure within 2 days and will be able to begin to return to normal life. The goal of our study is to assess the feasibility and tolerability of VATS for lung metastasis and eventually deliver this care as an outpatient procedure. unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description: Participation involves an initial staging visit and 5 follow up visits. unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Efficacy and safety of a novel anti-cancer therapeutic for the treatment of metastatic mammary carcinoma in cats
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description: Purpose of Study:Mammary tumors are a commonly encountered cancer in cats, particularly in females, with 80-90% of masses diagnosed as malignant (carcinoma). Mammary carcinoma in cats parallels breast cancer in humans with regards to receptor expression profile and propensity of metastasis. The median survival time in cats ranges from 6 months to several years, depending on tumor size and grade. Greater than 60% of cats have more than one tumor at diagnosis, with the majority being high grade. The objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and efficacy of a novel therapeutic targeting miR-10b, a molecule responsible for viability of metastatic cells in cats with mammary carcinoma. This multipurpose therapy has a previously demonstrated efficacy in halting breast cancer invasion and metastasis in mice. The advantage of our novel therapeutic over existing drugs is that it can also be used to visualize primary and metastatic lesions in vivo by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Studies in cats with mammary carcinoma will help bring this therapeutic into clinic to treat human breast cancer.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: CAR T Cell and Verdinexor Therapy for Treatment of Glioma Tumors in Dogs
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
About the study


Every year, about 3 out of every 100 dogs will be diagnosed with a brain tumor. Many of these dogs will be diagnosed with a glioma tumor, which is the second most common type of brain tumor and also, unfortunately, the most difficult to treat. One of the most promising developing areas of research for treating glioma tumors is immunotherapy, which is a type of intervention that uses the dog's own cells to fight the cancer cells.


This study is looking at a specific type of immunotherapy called CAR T cell therapy. CAR T cells are created by doing a simple blood draw from the dog to extract the T cells ("fighter" cells), which are then infused with a Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR) protein. This "upgrade" allows the T cells to target and attack the glioma tumor cells. This intervention has been used in children with brain tumors but this study will be the first time it's being used in dogs with glioma tumors!


In addition to the immunotherapy, we will be looking at a specific type of chemotherapy that has shown extremely promising results in canine lymphoma, along with human glioma tumors. This chemotherapy drug, verdinexor, will be used in combination with the CAR T cell therapy in an effort to produce the best possible outcome.


Who qualifies


Dogs who are over 10kg (22lb) in body weight who have already had a brain tumor diagnosed on MRI.

Tumor must be surgically accessible to allow for biopsy and injection of CAR T cells directly into the tumor

Dogs must be healthy enough to safely undergo anesthesia for the biopsy of the tumor

Dogs cannot have previously received chemotherapy or radiation for this tumor


Study activities and Timeline


Visit 1 | Day-17

  1. Exam
  2. Blood draw to create CAR T cells
  3. Begin verdinexor (chemo) therapy twice per week

Visit 2 | Days -4 and -3

  1. On both days, we will give a drug that temporarily depletes the immune system to prepare your dog's body for the CAR T cell injection

Visit 3 | Days 0, 1, and 3

  1. The first day will consist of the first CAR T cell injection while the next 2 days consist of recheck exams

Visit 4 | Days 8 - 10

  1. The visits throughout these days will consist of a brief planning scan followed by the brain biopsy surgery. During the surgery, a second injection of CAR T cells will be given directly into the tumor.

Visit 5 | Month 3

  1. We will do a recheck a MRI to evaluate the tumor response


Verdinexor will continue to be given at home twice weekly until the tumor progresses based on neurological signs or growth seen on MRI.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Electrochemotherapy for Nasal Cancer
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Nasal Cancers in dogs and cats are uncommon and standard treatment is external beam radiation therapy. Side effects from radiation therapy may sometimes be severe and not every patient will qualify or respond to this therapy. Plus, there are significant delays in accommodating patients for timely radiation therapy treatment due to the paucity of centers and available specialists.


Nasal Electrochemotherapy has been used predominantly outside of the United States (see below).


Radiol Oncol 2017 Nov 1;51(4):422-430.

 doi: 10.1515/raon-2017-0043. eCollection 2017 Dec.

Minimally Invasive Electrochemotherapy Procedure for Treating Nasal Duct Tumors in Dogs using a Single Needle Electrode

Felipe Maglietti 1 2 3, Matías Tellado 4, Nahuel Olaiz 1 2 3, Sebastian Michinski 1 2 3, Guillermo Marshall 1 2 3


Abstract

Background: Nasal cavity tumors are usually diagnosed late, when they already have infiltrated adjacent tissues thus requiring very aggressive treatments with serious side effects. Here we use electrochemotherapy (ECT), a well demonstrated treatment modality for superficial tumors.

Materials and methods: In the case of deep-seated tumors, the main limitation of ECT is reaching the tumor with an appropriate electric field. To overcome this limitation we introduce the single needle electrode (SiNE), a minimally invasive device that can deliver an appropriate electric field with a simple procedure. Twenty-one canine patients with spontaneous tumors were selected, eleven were treated using the SiNE with ECT, and ten with surgery plus adjuvant chemotherapy as a control group.

Results: In the SiNE group, 27% achieved a complete response, 64% had a partial response, and 9% had a stable disease. This means that 91% of objective responses were obtained. The mean overall survival was 16.86 months (4-32 months, median 16.5 months), with a survival rate significantly higher (p = 0.0008) when compared with control group. The only side effect observed was the inflammation of the treated nasal passage, which was controlled with corticosteroid therapy for one week. One year after the treatment, 60% of the canine of the SiNE group vs. 10% of the control group remained alive, and after the 32 months follow-up, the survival rate were 30% and 0%, respectively.

Conclusions: ECT with the SiNE can be safely used in canine to treat nasal tumors with encouraging results.


We now have a nasal electrochemotherapy electrode here in the United States.


Clinical Protocol involves selected patients to receive a short sedation with IV propofol, +/- dexdomitor and O2 via intubation. Bleomycin IV 8 minutes prior to electrode placement into both nares providing a short pulse which opens the cell membranes driving chemotherapy to the region being treated. In this case, we begin treatment at the deepest point of the nasal cavity just proximal to the region of the cribiform plate (end of nasal cavity). After each treatment, the electrode is moved proximally until the entire region of both nasal cavities are treated. Side effects are minimal and patients will go home on 3 days of anti-inflammatory medication. This is an out-patient procedure.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: PSMA Ligand Based Theranostic to Treat Canine Prostatic Cancer
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
In this study, we will test a new research medication that combines a chemotherapy drug called MMAE (monomethyl Auristatin E) and a light-sensitive drug (Pc-413) and a laser light source (photodynamic therapy) to kill cancer cells in the prostate and in other areas of the body (metastatic disease). These two agents are linked to a molecule that binds to PSMA (prostate specific membrane antigen), a cell surface marker that is produced by prostatic cancer in large quantities. The research medication is inactive until it binds to PSMA. When the research medication binds to PSMA it is taken into the cell and activated. This means the research medication is targeted specifically to prostate cancer cells. The overall goal is to use this new research medication that is specific to prostate cancer cells to kill the cancer.


This study will cover the specific study related diagnostics once your dog is enrolled:

• Chest X-rays

• Abdominal ultrasound

• Prostate aspirate

• Blood work (CBC and chemistry)

• Urinalysis

• Physical examination


All costs associated with the theranostic infusions and laser will be covered by the study including the fees associated with hospitalization. The study will cover the cost of the recheck visits every 2 months following the treatments, including the physical examination, blood work, urinalysis, chest x-rays and abdominal ultrasound fees. If your dog needs sedation for any of the study related procedures, the study will cover the cost of the sedation as well.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Radiation + Targeted Therapy for Bladder Cancer in Dogs
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Transitional cell carcinoma (TCC) is the most common form of bladder tumors in dogs. Fractionated radiation therapy is one of the most effective treatment options for this form of tumor, and is typically combined with chemotherapy and an NSAID medication. Lapatinib is a newer therapy that has been used as a single agent for the treatment of dogs with this form of bladder tumor. The goal of this trial is to see if the combination of radiation therapy and lapatinib will be safe and well tolerated in dogs with TCC.


If your dog participates in this study, they will receive oral lapatinib through the course of the approximately 4-month study, as well as oral NSAIDs. 5-7 days after starting these medications, they will also complete 15 daily (M-F) fractions of radiation therapy, which requires daily general anesthesia. Patients will get a urinary ultrasound at the beginning and end of the study, which may require sedation for some patients. They will also receive routine bloodwork throughout the course of the study, as well as blood collection at the beginning of radiation, end of radiation, and the conclusion of the study for study purposes.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Characterization of Soft Tissue Sarcoma Microscopic Extension
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
The goal of the study is to assess the microscopic extension of soft tissue sarcomas. The enrollment will be limited to dogs cytologically or histologically diagnosed soft tissue sarcomas that are undergoing a wide excision. Wide surgical excision, defined as three-centimeter lateral margins and of layer of fascia (dense tissue) deep to the mass, will be performed as the standard of care. While under general anesthesia and immediately prior to routine surgery, sterile tattoo ink will be used to mark specific margins around the tumor. All tattoo ink will be within the tumor sample and planned margin with no tattoo ink applied outside the tissue to be removed.


There are no additional costs associated with the study beyond those acquired through routine care for the underlying condition. The study provides only costs toward the surgical procedure (mass removal) itself and the histopathology (biopsy) charges. This combination of charges would typically be $441-$1074 depending on tumor size. All other costs are the responsibility of the owner.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Finding draining lymph nodes for anal gland tumors in dogs using minimally invasive surgery
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description: Anal sac cancers in dogs often spread to other areas of the body. This is called metastasis. Local lymph nodes are a common site for the cancer to spread in dogs with anal sac tumors. Removing lymph nodes with cancer improves outcome. However, assessment of the lymph nodes that drain fluid from a tumor can be challenging. A safe and common test is sentinel lymph node (SLN) mapping. This is where we test the first lymph node(s) that drain fluid from a tumor for cancer cells. It has been used in dogs with anal sac cancer. However, the lymph nodes that drain anal sac tumors are located within the abdomen and pelvis. So far SLN mapping on dogs with anal sac tumors has needed open abdominal surgery. Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) has many reported benefits for patients compared to open abdominal surgery, including smaller incisions, reduced pain, and earlier return to function. This is where small incisions are made for cameras and instruments, and tissue can be removed without making a large incision. We have successfully done SLN mapping for anal sac cancer with MIS techniques in dog cadavers. We want to evaluate these SLN mapping techniques via a MIS approach in dogs with anal sac tumors. We also want to see how this compares to a previously studied method called CT-lymphography that is done before surgery. Our goal is to obtain important cancer care information from SLN mapping, but with the potential benefits of MIS compared to open abdominal surgery.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: 3D-Printed Implant that Replaces Bone for Limb Sparing in Giant Breed Dogs with a Primary Bone Tumor
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Although limb sparing for bone tumors has been performed for over 30 years in dogs, the complication rate for this surgery remains high. Risks of the surgery include infection, problems related to the implants, and local recurrence. Many factors are contributing to the high rate of complications and one of them is likely the material used to fabricate the implants. We hypothesize that if the implant used to replace the segment of bone with the tumor (i.e. endoprosthesis) was made of a material that the body could replace with its own viable bone, many of the complications would not occur or would be easier to treat.


3D-printing can create personalized implants made of a material that the body can replace with its own bone, namely anorganic (deproteinized) bone mineral (ABM). Over a period of time, the body can grow new viable bone while removing the ABM, such that the metal plate and screws used with limb sparing would be able to be removed after a period of time, leaving the dog with only its own tissues. The goal of this study is to evaluate a novel personalized implant system for limb sparing in dogs with primary bone tumors and identify complications associated with this surgical approach.


Dogs will undergo imaging with a PET-CT scan, which is a special form of imaging that involves giving a small dose of a radioactive substance to help identify any areas of cancer spread. The data from this imaging will also be used to create the patient-specific implant and tools for surgery, which is anticipated to take 5 days or less. Once the supplies are ready, the limb sparing surgical procedure will be performed. Dogs will return two weeks after surgery for suture removal and to start carboplatin chemotherapy as long as the surgical site is well-healed. Carboplatin will be given every 3 weeks for 6 treatments, and dogs will be followed for up to 20 months after surgery. X-rays of the chest and limb will be performed every 8 weeks for the duration of the study, and force plate gait analysis will be done every 6 months. Some of these follow-up visits can be done with your regular veterinarian if you choose; however, the study will not be able to cover the costs of these visits.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Targeted Radiopharmaceutical Therapy (RPT) in Companion Dogs with Peripheral T-Cell Lymphoma (PTCL)
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
In collaboration with the UW Carbone Cancer Center, we are developing an innovative treatment for canine Peripheral T-cell Lymphoma (PTCL). This study aims to evaluate the safety, effectiveness, and optimal dosage of ⁹⁰Y-NM600 targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) in dogs with PTCL. Our research indicates that targeted RPT can effectively reach tumors, regardless of tumor location.


Please note that this is not a double-masked trial; ALL enrolled patients will receive the targeted RPT.


This funded study (after initial screening) covers the following expenses:

Please note that the standard of care chemotherapy is NOT part of the trial.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Clinical Trial of Trametinib in Dogs with Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML)
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Dogs can develop a serious blood cancer called acute myeloid leukemia (AML). This disease often gets worse quickly, and there is no standard treatment that reliably helps dogs live longer.

This study is testing a drug called trametinib to see if it may help dogs with AML. Trametinib is a medication used in people to treat some cancers. It works by blocking signals that help cancer cells grow. This drug is experimental for use in dogs with AML, and its safety and effectiveness for this condition are not yet known. In this study, all dogs will receive trametinib along with prednisone, which is commonly used to help dogs with leukemia feel better. About 13 dogs are expected to take part in this study.


Treatment is done with your local oncologist. As part of this study, pets will have the following things done:

• A physical exam by a veterinarian

• Blood tests to check blood counts and organ health

• Urine tests

• A cheek (buccal) swab to collect DNA for future research studies related to leukemia and treatment response

• Regular follow-up visits approximately 1 week and 2 weeks after starting treatment, approximately every 2 weeks through Week 12, and approximately every 4 weeks thereafter while dogs remains on study

• Dogs will take trametinib by mouth once daily at home

• Dogs will also take prednisone as directed by your veterinarian

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Osteosarcoma- Targeted Bone Electrochemotherapy with Cementoplasty; Alternative to Amputation
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Canine appendicular osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone tumor in dogs. Standard treatment is amputation and chemotherapy with median survival around 13 months. Some patients are not candidates for amputation due to obesity, orthopedic conditions or other mitigating circumstances. Limb sparing is another option but limited in availability and is considered invasive.


Targeted bone electrochemotherapy (ECT-B) is an emerging focused cancer treatment therapy predominantly utilized in people with metastatic cancer to bone as a component of reducing bone pain and retarding tumor growth. It involves the insertion of a single pole electrode into the tumor and drawing chemotherapy directly to the tumor. In addition, once treatment is rendered, the remaining bone defect will be filled via sterile orthopedic bone cement, the patient recovered and discharged the same day.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Developing a Blood Test for Early Detection of Bone Cancer Relapse
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Osteosarcoma is the most common primary bone cancer in dogs, specially in large size breeds and it presents a high biological aggressiveness, in many cases at the time of diagnosis, metastatic dissemination has already occurred. Currently, the standard of care consists of surgical excision of the affected limb, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy. However, despite initial therapeutic response, patients develop treatment resistance, leading to the presence of metastasis, most commonly within the lungs, reducing life expectancy and quality of life of the patient. 

Recently the use of liquid biopsies, a minimally invasive sample collection from body fluids, such as blood, has been increasing, as they detect specific molecular biomarkers. Liquid biopsies can aid in the detection of certain pathologies, monitor disease progression or recurrence after the treatment, the latter can be achieved by measuring molecules such as proteins and microRNAs that are in the circulating blood. These proteins and microRNA might provide less invasive and faster detection than other techniques, such as computerized tomography (CT scan). 

For our research the main goal is to determine if this blood test is able to predict osteosarcoma recurrence, as these biomarkers may provide an earlier status of relapse, and could aid in designing more effective treatments. To support this, our team is developing a lab-on-a-chip platform that can measure the selected biomarkers using a minimal volume of blood. To achieve the previous, we are looking for canine patients, over 25 kg (55.11 lbs) that have been diagnosed with appendicular osteosarcoma, and have not undergone amputation of the affected limb.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Using a Fluorescent Dye to Identify Bladder Tumors in Dogs During Surgery
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Urothelial carcinoma (UC) is the most common type of bladder cancer in dogs. For dogs with tumors in certain locations, surgical removal (partial cystectomy) can improve outcomes with low risk. New minimally invasive techniques that maintain a closed bladder may offer additional benefits and warrant further investigation, but these approaches currently rely on specialized camera equipment within the bladder, which is not always available, to identify tumors. This pilot study will test whether a safe dye, indocyanine green (ICG), used with near-infrared (NIR) imaging can identify bladder tumors and their edges during surgery. The findings with NIR will be compared with what is seen by the surgeon and with microscopic examination by a pathologist. Results will be incorporated into future studies with novel surgical techniques that have the potential to improve outcomes in dogs with UC.


Dogs enrolled in the study will receive a single intravenous injection of ICG approximately 24 hours before their planned surgery for bladder tumor removal, and a special near-infrared camera will be used during the procedure to assess whether the tumor and its margins fluoresce differently than surrounding normal tissue. ICG is an FDA-approved dye that is commonly used for other imaging purposes in human and veterinary medicine, but its use for identifying bladder tumors during surgery in dogs is considered investigational and its effectiveness for this purpose has not yet been established. A total of five dogs will be enrolled in this study, and all dogs will receive the same dye injection and imaging procedure during their planned surgery; there are no separate treatment or control groups. Study participation is complete after surgery is performed.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: CARE Trial: Combined Autophagy inhibition and Radiation therapy to improve Efficacy in Canine Glioma
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Dogs diagnosed with glioma, an aggressive brain tumor, often experience limited benefit from standard treatments such as radiation therapy alone. This clinical trial is evaluating a novel investigational drug called bisaminoquinoline-13 (BAQ-13) that may help improve how brain tumors respond to radiation therapy.


BAQ-13 works by blocking a process called autophagy, which cancer cells use to survive treatment. This study will evaluate whether BAQ-13 can safely reach brain tumors, be tolerated by dogs receiving radiation therapy, and show early signs of effectiveness.


What happens in this study

  1. An initial screening and eligibility workup, including physical and neurologic examination, blood work, and diagnostic imaging


  1. Advanced brain imaging (MRI and CT scans) performed under general anesthesia


  1. Minimally invasive brain tumor biopsies performed at enrollment and after treatment


  1. Intravenous administration of an investigational drug (BAQ-13) twice weekly for 4 weeks


  1. Concurrent radiation therapy (standard of care)


  1. Blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample collection at specified time points


  1. Overnight hospitalization following biopsy procedures


  1. Follow-up visits, including in-hospital evaluations and telemedicine check-ins


  1. Completion of owner questionnaires to monitor quality of life and treatment effects


  1. End of Study: When your family is ready to elect humane euthanasia, your dog will return to UC Davis. A brief examination will be performed prior to humane euthanasia. Following your dog’s death, a brain MRI will be performed, and they will undergo a routine necropsy. We will evaluate distribution of the drug in the brain, brain tumor, and vital organs (heart, lung, kidneys, liver). If your dog passes away or is euthanized elsewhere, the study team will arrange return to UC Davis for post-mortem evaluation.



IACUC: 24515

Study number: VCCT-26-001

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: Single Dose Plasma Pharmacokinetic Analysis of Targeted Anticancer Agents in Tumor Bearing Dogs
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description:
Multiple companies are offering services that recommend "targeted therapy" for dogs with cancer, using drugs that are approved for the treatment of some types of cancer in humans. However, most of these drugs have not been studied for effectiveness in dogs, nor do we know how much or how often they should be given. The goal of this study is to measure levels over 24-96 hours of these drugs following a single oral or subcutaneous dose, in pet dogs with cancer. Dogs will receive a single oral or subcutaneous dose of a given agent at the dose recommended by the company, followed by blood collection 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8 and 24 hours later. Following the 24-hour blood collection, dogs will be off study and eligible for any other treatment.


Your dog will receive a single oral dose of one of these drugs at a dose that is predicted to cause no side effects. A small amount of blood (approximately 1 teaspoon) will be collected at the time points above. Collection of the blood samples will take all day. Your dog will need to return the following day for 1 additional blood draw, or alternatively, they can stay overnight at no cost to you. Some dogs will need to return for blood collection 48 and 96 hours after administration. After the 24-hour blood sample is drawn, the study is over and your dog is eligible to receive any additional treatment that is recommended.


Although the drugs we are studying have caused minimal side effects in laboratory dogs at the doses we are planning to use (even when given every day for several weeks), they have not been studied in pet dogs, which may be older and have other medical issues. Therefore, side effects (although extremely unlikely) could range from mild to severe, up to and including the death of your dog. Medications will be provided as needed to treat/prevent any side effects that might occur.


Costs covered by the clinical trial for eligible enrolled dogs include the cost of all examinations, drug dispensing, and blood collection. You will be responsible for the initial exam fee, and tests to confirm that your dog is eligible. Participating owners will receive a $500 credit to their dog’s Veterinary Teaching Hospital account, which can be applied to the initial testing or used to reduce costs of other cancer treatment when the study is complete.

unresolved_exact_url_candidates.name: CHOP vs. LOPP chemotherapy as a first line treatment for naïve peripheral T cell lymphoma in dogs
unresolved_exact_url_candidates.description: Lymphoma comprises approximately 25% of all canine cancers. Up to 40% of these cases are caused by T lymphocytes, known as peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL). The vast majority of lymphoma cases cannot be addressed with surgery and instead warrant chemotherapy. The standard of care chemotherapy protocol for lymphoma is abbreviated CHOP, which stands for the 4 drugs involved. Generally, dogs with PTCL treated with CHOP chemotherapy tend to experience shorter remission durations and overall survival than dogs with diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL). When treated with CHOP chemotherapy, PTCL dogs have a median survival time of 4-9 months while DLBCL dogs have a median survival time of 11-13 months. Previous studies have questioned whether other, non-CHOP protocols may be better suited for dogs with PTCL in hopes of increasing remission and survival times. One protocol that has been repeatedly investigated is LOPP chemotherapy. This protocol uses two of the same drugs as CHOP and two that are different. Recent studies have demonstrated with dogs with PTCL treated with LOPP can experience survival times closer to 11-17 months. While these findings are promising, none of these investigations have had a control arm of dogs receiving CHOP chemotherapy. The purpose of this study is to provide a direct comparison between the outcomes for dogs with peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL) treated with CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. The findings of this study could help veterinarians understand if one protocol is truly superior to the other for dogs with PTCL. In this study, your dog will be randomly selected to receive either CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. At each visit, their lymph node size, blood work, and overall wellbeing will be assessed. Both protocols involve treatments every 7-14 days and take 4-6 months to complete. Following protocol completion, your pet will return once monthly to assess remission status.
